descriptions.vowel_reduction: A full vowel reduces to schwa in an unstressed syllable. does → dəz
descriptions.monophthongization: A diphthong is realized as a plain vowel. my → ma
descriptions.elision_syllable: A whole syllable is lost. probably → pɹɑbli, camera → kæmɹə
descriptions.word_elision: The word leaves no acoustic trace: fast speech swallows it.
descriptions.flapping: /t/ or /d/ between vowels sounds like a soft r. water → wɔɾɚ
descriptions.t_deletion: A final /t/ or /d/ drops out of a consonant cluster. next day → nɛks deɪ
descriptions.t_unreleased: A final /t/ or /d/ closes but is never released: an unreleased [t̚]. (The espeak engine cannot hear the closure and infers it from a /t/ missing after a vowel.) that → ðæt̚
descriptions.glottalization: /t/ closes into a glottal stop. button → bʌʔn̩
descriptions.th_stopping: θ and ð are pronounced as the stops t/d. that → dat
descriptions.palatalization: t+j and d+j merge into tʃ/dʒ at the end of a word. got you → gotcha
descriptions.linking: The word runs into the next vowel: a final consonant (does it → dʌ‿zɪt), an r (far away → fɑɹ‿əweɪ) or a w/j glide (go on → ɡoʊ‿wɑn).
descriptions.h_dropping: The unstressed h disappears. tell him → tell im
descriptions.contraction_lex: A lexicalized reduced form. want to → wanna
descriptions.place_assimilation: A final n/t/d takes the place of the next consonant. ten bucks → tɛm bʌks, in case → ɪŋ keɪs
descriptions.nt_reduction: /nt/ before a vowel loses its /t/: a plain n or a nasal flap. twenty → twɛni, winter → wɪɾ̃ɚ
descriptions.function_elision: A function word loses a consonant as well as its vowel. of → ə, them → əm

vowel_reduction.why: Unstressed vowels turning to schwa is the engine of English rhythm, and the first thing the report says to produce (§4, stage 2).

monophthongization.why: Diphthongs flattened into one vowel (Southern /aɪ/ → [aː]) are regional (§5): recognize them, don't imitate them.

elision_syllable.why: Schwa deletion (famly, prob'ly, camra) is very common but casual: understanding it comes first (§3E, §5).

word_elision.why: A word swallowed by fast speech: something to hear, not to aim for.

flapping.why: Safe to produce and one of the most rewarding things to learn (§3A).

t_deletion.why: Dropping the t/d of a cluster (next day, old man) belongs to casual speech; all dialects do it before a consonant (§3E, §5).

t_unreleased.why: A final /t/ held without a burst (what, that) is the everyday American form; releasing it fully sounds over-careful (§3B).

glottalization.why: Safe before a syllabic n (button, important — stage 3); before a vowel it is optional and led by young Western speakers (§3B).

th_stopping.why: th → d/t is an AAVE and regional feature (§5): recognize it; a learner should keep working on θ/ð instead (§7).

palatalization.why: didja, gotcha, doncha are universal and safe to produce (§3D).

linking.why: Consonant–vowel linking, linking r and the w/j glides are fundamental to fluency and safe to produce (§3G).

h_dropping.why: Safe in unstressed pronouns and auxiliaries — but never at the start of a sentence (§3C).

contraction_lex.why: gonna, wanna, gotta, gimme, lemme, kinda are universal and safe; some forms are marked — see each form (§1).

place_assimilation.why: tem bucks, ing case happen only in fast, natural speech; forced, they sound odd (§3F, §7).

nt_reduction.why: winter → winner is very American and widespread but variable; the report files it under understand only (§5).

function_elision.why: of → ə and them → əm are the weak forms the report says to produce (§2, stage 2): lotsa, kinda, tell 'em.

deviate.source: Johnson 2004, Massive reduction in conversational American English (ViC/Buckeye, ~88,000 words)
deviate.note: words that depart from their citation form in at least one segment

segment_loss.note: words that lose at least one whole segment

syllable_loss.note: words that lose at least one syllable: about one word in 20

schwa_share.source: pedagogical estimates quoted in the report (practiceme.app: ~1 in 5 vowels; learnenglishsounds.com: ~25 % of syllables in connected speech)
schwa_share.note: schwa is the most frequent vowel of spoken English

function_words.note: about half of what is heard is a function word, reduced by default

flapping.source: Patterson & Connine 2001, Phonetica 58:254–275 (Switchboard: Northern 74.8 %, North Midland 81.6 %); 99 % in read speech (Zue & Laferriere 1979)
flapping.note: flapped /t, d/ in the flapping context (after a vowel or /r/, before an unstressed vowel)

glottal_prevocalic.source: Eddington & Channer 2010, American Speech 85.3:338–351 (Santa Barbara Corpus: 262 of 1,101 word-final prevocalic /t/)
glottal_prevocalic.note: word-final /t/ before a vowel realized as a glottal stop; higher in young Western speakers

metric_labels.deviate: words that differ from the citation form
metric_labels.segment_loss: words that lose a whole segment
metric_labels.weak_forms: function words in their weak form
metric_labels.flapping: t/d flapped where flapping can happen
metric_labels.glottal_before_syllabic_n: glottal t before a syllabic n (button)
metric_labels.glottal_prevocalic: final t before a vowel as a glottal stop

phone_engine_notes.timit61: Narrow phonetic recognizer (TIMIT-61): hears flaps, glottal stops, unreleased stops and weak forms. Weights Apache-2.0; trained on TIMIT (LDC), whose data is licensed for non-commercial research.
phone_engine_notes.espeak: The original engine (wav2vec2 trained on espeak-ng transcriptions). Unrestricted training data, but it tends to hear the dictionary form instead of what was said.
